title: Hiding in the night sky
caption: The low surface brightness galaxy UGC 477, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: UGC 477 · constellation Pisces · about 110 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble image shows UGC 477, a galaxy in Pisces lying just over 110 million light-years from Earth. It is a low surface brightness galaxy, a type whose light is spread thinly, making it far more diffuse than galaxies such as Andromeda or the Milky Way.

Their surface brightness can be as much as 250 times fainter than the night sky itself, so they are very hard to detect. Mike Disney proposed they existed in 1976, but they were only confirmed in 1986, with the discovery of the galaxy Malin 1.

Most of their matter is hydrogen gas, not stars, and their centers lack the crowd of stars found in the bulges of normal spirals. Astronomers suspect this is because they tend to sit in empty regions, where fewer encounters and mergers have triggered intense star formation. They appear to be dominated by dark matter.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.38 x 2.69 arcminutes) and distance (110 million light years), the frame spans roughly 108,000 × 86,000 light-years. Its light set out about 110 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using filters at 475 and 775 nm, in visible and near-infrared light. The colors assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: A galaxy fainter than the night sky's own glow is effectively invisible to the eye. Only long, sensitive exposures reveal it.

explore: That makes galaxies like UGC 477 useful for studying dark matter, the invisible substance thought to make up much of the mass in galaxies. Because they are so faint, they have long been underrepresented in galaxy surveys, and their importance has been recognized only fairly recently.
alt: A faint, diffuse galaxy seen by Hubble.
